breath_title: Who (and what) is in the room with our learners?
breath_text: Generative AI is now a reasoning partner at the bedside, so the authors of this week's top read argue we should teach and supervise the learner-AI pair, with graduated autonomy, not just the learner. Coaches who keep students tied to their values ease the jump to residency. And a growing share of the doctors our residents train beside come from Caribbean schools, most into primary care.

top.headline: Teach the learner-AI pair: redesigning clinical reasoning education for generative AI
bullets: Scholarly Perspective: GAI is an "out-in-the-world" reasoning tool, so the unit of learning shifts from the individual learner to the learner-AI pair, with room for upskilling but also never-skilling, mis-skilling, and deskilling.

Vignettes across training stages lead to 5 redesign strategies: introduce GAI early, keep reasoning-first workflows, grant graduated autonomy for GAI use in care, train faculty to supervise GAI-assisted reasoning, and rethink assessment.
top.tip: treat AI use like any other entrustment decision on your team: talk about when learners use it on their own and when they reason first and check after.
top.citation: Schaye VE, Parsons AS, Olson APJ, Abdulnour RE, Daniel M. Acad Med. Online Oct 8, 2026. doi:10.1093/acamed/wvag318

top.headline: What a longitudinal coach adds on the road to residency
bullets: Qualitative focus groups at Tufts (Apr-Jul 2025) with graduating students, coaches, and deans of student affairs.

4 core coaching moves: values-based reflection, emotional support, respecting student agency, and nudging students to a broader advising network. All 3 groups stressed validating students and keeping them tied to their values.
top.tip: these moves map onto how we onboard interns. Asking about values on day 1 may pay off.
top.citation: Boehm L, Blanco M, Hayes V, et al. Acad Med. Online Oct 10, 2026. doi:10.1093/acamed/wvag322

top.headline: Caribbean medical schools: about 1 in 20 licensed US physicians
bullets: ACGME residency data (2013-2023) plus FSMB licensure data: first US licenses to Caribbean grads rose from 33 in 1980 to 2,768 in 2024; 49,256 now hold a license (~5% of licensed physicians).
Caribbean grads train in family medicine at more than twice the rate of US/Canadian grads and other IMGs, and are younger (mean age 44.1 vs 51.5 and 55.2).
top.tip: a big, growing primary care pipeline. The authors call for accreditation-mandated transparency on student outcomes.
top.citation: Gruppuso PA, Pei X, Arnhart K, et al. Acad Med. Online Oct 8, 2026. doi:10.1093/acamed/wvag317
